title: Life's slow recovery after the Great Dying
summary: After the end-Permian extinction, hot, oxygen-poor seas and sparse lands hosted few species for millions of years, led on land by Lystrosaurus.
description: The Early Triassic opened on a devastated planet: the end-Permian extinction had removed most marine species, and complex ecosystems took roughly 5–10 million years to rebuild. Oxygen isotopes from conodont fossils suggest extreme greenhouse heat, with tropical sea surfaces perhaps near 40 °C, leaving an equatorial belt that many animals avoided. So-called disaster taxa flourished in the gap: the stocky, beaked dicynodont Lystrosaurus became one of the commonest land vertebrates, found from South Africa's Karoo Basin to Antarctica, India and China. Coral reefs and coal-forming forests were largely absent for millions of years, and repeated carbon-cycle upheavals punctuated the interval. The pace of recovery varied between groups and is still actively studied: ammonoids rebounded quickly, while reef builders and many land plants lagged.

title: Marine reptiles radiate after the Great Dying
summary: Within about four million years of the Great Dying, early ichthyosaur relatives such as Cartorhynchus swam the seas of what is now eastern China.
description: Fossils from Chaohu in Anhui Province, China, show that marine reptiles diversified remarkably soon after the end-Permian extinction. Cartorhynchus, a small, short-snouted ichthyosauriform about 248 million years old, may have been partly amphibious, while the early ichthyosaur Chaohusaurus was already giving birth to live young. Over the following tens of millions of years ichthyosaurs evolved dolphin-like bodies, and some Late Triassic forms grew to well over 15 m long. Together with sauropterygians, the group that later produced plesiosaurs, they established reptiles as the top predators of Mesozoic oceans.

title: Nyasasaurus: the earliest dinosaur?
summary: Bones from Tanzania's Manda Beds suggest the dinosaur lineage, or its closest relatives, had appeared by the Middle Triassic.
description: Nyasasaurus parringtoni, known from an upper arm bone and a few vertebrae collected in the 1930s and formally named in 2012, shows bone tissue and skeletal features indicating rapid, dinosaur-like growth. If it is a true dinosaur, it pushes the group's origin back 10–15 million years before the well-dated dinosaurs of South America. Its age, usually given as Anisian (about 243 million years), is itself uncertain. Other evidence points in the same direction: close dinosaur relatives such as Asilisaurus lived in the same region, and dinosauromorph footprints from Poland date back to the Early Triassic.
mainstreamView: Most palaeontologists agree that the dinosaur lineage originated in the Middle Triassic or earlier, but whether Nyasasaurus itself is a dinosaur or a near-relative cannot be settled from such fragmentary remains, and the age of the Manda Beds is also debated.

title: Carnian Pluvial Episode
summary: About two million years of global warming and intense rainfall, probably driven by Wrangellia volcanism, reshaped Triassic life and aided the rise of dinosaurs.
description: Around 234–232 million years ago, a series of carbon-cycle disturbances brought warmer and much wetter conditions across Pangaea, recorded by humid-climate sediments, soils and fossil turnover from the Italian Dolomites to England, China and Argentina. The most widely favoured trigger is the eruption of the Wrangellia large igneous province, now preserved in western North America. The episode coincided with significant extinctions among marine and land organisms. In its aftermath many modern groups appear or expand, including dinosaurs, the first calcareous nannoplankton, modern-type reef corals and several living conifer families. The episode was recognised as a distinct global event only from the late 1980s, and its exact duration, number of pulses and cause are still being refined.

title: Early dinosaurs: Eoraptor and Herrerasaurus
summary: In Argentina's Ischigualasto Formation, early dinosaurs such as Eoraptor and Herrerasaurus appear as modest members of faunas ruled by other reptiles.
description: The Ischigualasto Formation of north-western Argentina, radiometrically dated to about 231 million years ago, preserves some of the oldest undisputed dinosaurs, including the small omnivore Eoraptor, the predator Herrerasaurus and the early sauropodomorph Panphagia. Slightly older dinosaurs, such as Staurikosaurus and Buriolestes, come from the Santa Maria Formation of southern Brazil, about 233 million years old. These first dinosaurs were mostly bipedal and modest in size, and they were outnumbered by rhynchosaurs, cynodonts and crocodile-line archosaurs. Dinosaurs became ecologically dominant on land only after the Carnian Pluvial Episode and especially the end-Triassic extinction. The site forms part of the Ischigualasto/Talampaya UNESCO World Heritage Site.

title: First mammal relatives (mammaliaforms)
summary: Small, probably nocturnal mammaliaforms descended from cynodont therapsids appeared in the Late Triassic, forerunners of all mammals.
description: Mammals evolved from cynodonts, a group of therapsids that survived the end-Permian extinction. By the Late Triassic, shrew-sized mammaliaforms with a new jaw joint and specialised teeth had appeared; Adelobasileus, known from a partial skull from the Tecovas Formation of Texas about 225 million years old, is among the earliest candidates. Better-known early forms such as Morganucodon and Kuehneotherium lived around the Triassic–Jurassic boundary in Europe, China and elsewhere. Many were probably nocturnal insectivores, a lifestyle that may have shaped mammalian traits such as acute hearing, smell and warm-bloodedness. Where to draw the line between mammals and their near relatives, and when the first crown-group mammals appeared, remain debated.

title: Turtles get their shells: Odontochelys
summary: Odontochelys, a toothed turtle from Guizhou, China, had a full belly shell but only a partial back shell, revealing how the turtle shell was built.
description: Odontochelys semitestacea, described in 2008 from Late Triassic (Carnian) coastal marine deposits of the Guanling biota in Guizhou, southern China, still had teeth and a complete belly shell, or plastron, but no full carapace: its back was covered only by broadened ribs. It suggests that the shell was assembled in stages, a sequence supported by Pappochelys, a turtle relative about 240 million years old from southern Germany, and possibly by the Permian Eunotosaurus from South Africa, which already had widened ribs. By about 210 million years ago Proganochelys, also from Germany, had a fully formed shell, although it could not yet pull in its head. Whether the first turtles evolved in water or on land, perhaps as burrowers, is still debated, as is their exact place among reptiles, though most genetic studies now group them with archosaurs, the lineage of crocodiles and birds.

title: Pterosaurs: first vertebrates with powered flight
summary: Pterosaurs such as Eudimorphodon, found near Bergamo, Italy, became the first vertebrates to achieve powered flight.
description: Pterosaurs were archosaurs with wings of skin stretched from an enormously elongated fourth finger, and they flew some 60 million years before the first birds. Among the oldest well-preserved examples is Eudimorphodon from the Late Triassic Zorzino Limestone of Lombardy, about 210 million years old, a small, long-tailed fish-eater with many-cusped teeth. Their origins long puzzled researchers because no transitional forms were known; in 2020 lagerpetids, small Triassic reptiles closely related to dinosaurs, were identified as their nearest relatives. Pterosaurs persisted throughout the Mesozoic, culminating in giants such as Quetzalcoatlus, before vanishing in the end-Cretaceous extinction.

title: Manicouagan impact
summary: An asteroid about 5 km wide struck what is now Quebec, leaving one of Earth's largest preserved craters, now a ring-shaped lake about 70 km across.
description: The Manicouagan structure in Quebec, Canada, was formed by an impact dated to about 214 million years ago, during the Norian stage of the Late Triassic. The original crater was roughly 100 km wide; erosion and glaciation have left an annular reservoir about 70 km across around a central uplift, René-Levasseur Island, which is easily seen from orbit. It was once proposed as a cause of the end-Triassic extinction, but precise dating places it some 13 million years earlier, and no mass extinction coincides with it. A 1998 proposal that it formed part of a chain of simultaneous impacts has been undermined by later re-dating of the other craters.

title: Central Atlantic Magmatic Province erupts
summary: As Pangaea began to split, floods of basalt erupted across what are now four continents, forming one of the largest volcanic provinces on Earth.
description: The Central Atlantic Magmatic Province (CAMP) consists of lava flows, sills and dykes now found in eastern North America, north-western Africa, Iberia and northern South America, which were joined within Pangaea when they formed. Originally covering perhaps 10 million km², it is among the largest volcanic provinces known, and most of it was emplaced in several pulses over roughly 600,000 years around 201 million years ago. Uranium–lead dating shows that its onset coincided with the end-Triassic extinction, making CAMP the leading suspect for that crisis. It is exposed in places such as the Palisades along New York's Hudson River and the Argana and High Atlas basins of Morocco, and it marks the rifting that would soon open the central Atlantic Ocean.

title: End-Triassic mass extinction
summary: One of the 'Big Five' mass extinctions wiped out roughly three-quarters of species, clearing the way for dinosaurs to dominate the Jurassic.
description: About 201.4 million years ago, at the boundary between the Triassic and Jurassic periods, an estimated 70–80% of species disappeared, including the last conodonts, most large amphibians and many crocodile-line archosaurs, while reefs and ammonoids suffered heavy losses. The extinction coincides closely with the first eruptions of the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province, and most researchers attribute it to massive volcanic release of carbon dioxide, and possibly sulphur and methane, causing rapid warming, ocean acidification and oxygen loss. The main extinction pulse appears to have been geologically rapid, perhaps unfolding over tens of thousands of years. Dinosaurs survived and, with many competitors gone, diversified and grew larger in the Early Jurassic. The exact kill mechanisms and the relative roles of warming, acidification and volcanic cooling remain debated.

title: The Mesozoic marine revolution
dateLabel: c. 200–66 million years ago (peaking in the Cretaceous)
summary: Shell-crushing and shell-drilling predators multiplied in Mesozoic seas, and their prey evolved thicker, spinier shells or burrowed deeper.
description: Through the Jurassic and especially the Cretaceous, marine predators able to crush, drill or pry open shells became far more diverse and abundant, among them rays and sharks with pavement-like teeth, shell-crushing bony fishes, crabs and lobsters with powerful claws, drilling snails, starfish that pull bivalves apart and mosasaurs such as Globidens with bulbous crushing teeth. Their prey responded with thicker, spinier and more tightly coiled shells, narrower shell openings and deeper burrowing, while many stalked crinoids and brachiopods became rarer on shallow seafloors and persisted mainly in deeper water. The palaeontologist Geerat Vermeij named this escalation the Mesozoic marine revolution in 1977, building on earlier work by Steven Stanley on burrowing bivalves. Later studies found signs of a first phase as early as the Middle Triassic, and the relative roles of predation, rising productivity and changing seas in driving it are still studied. The arms race largely set up the predator–prey structure of modern marine communities.

title: Pangaea splits: the central Atlantic opens
summary: Seafloor spreading began between North America and north-west Africa, splitting Pangaea and creating a young central Atlantic Ocean.
description: After tens of millions of years of continental rifting, recorded by rift basins such as the Newark and Fundy basins, the supercontinent Pangaea began to break apart in the Early Jurassic. Oceanic crust started forming between North America and north-west Africa, creating a narrow central Atlantic that connected eastward with the Tethys Ocean. Estimates for the onset of seafloor spreading generally range between about 195 and 185 million years ago, because the oldest oceanic crust lacks clear magnetic anomalies. The Gulf of Mexico, which had been rifting since the Late Triassic, began forming oceanic crust only later, in the Late Jurassic, and the South and North Atlantic followed in the Cretaceous, progressively isolating the land faunas of the northern and southern continents.

title: Karoo–Ferrar eruptions and Gondwana's break-up
summary: Vast basalt eruptions in southern Africa and Antarctica marked the start of Gondwana's break-up into Africa, South America, Antarctica, India and Australia.
description: Around 183 million years ago, the Karoo and Ferrar large igneous provinces poured out basalts and intruded sills across what are now southern Africa, Antarctica and Tasmania; the thick lava pile of Lesotho's Drakensberg is a remnant. The eruptions accompanied rifting that would split the southern supercontinent Gondwana, first separating East Gondwana (Antarctica, India, Australia) from West Gondwana (Africa, South America) over the following tens of millions of years. Carbon released by the eruptions, particularly where magma intruded coal and organic-rich rocks, is widely linked to the contemporaneous Toarcian Oceanic Anoxic Event and its marine extinctions.

title: Toarcian Oceanic Anoxic Event
summary: Rapid warming and oxygen loss in the oceans caused a marine extinction and left black shales full of exquisite fossils, as at Holzmaden, Germany.
description: During the early Toarcian stage of the Early Jurassic, a sharp negative carbon-isotope excursion records a massive injection of light carbon into the ocean–atmosphere system, generally attributed to Karoo–Ferrar volcanism and possibly the release of methane. Seawater warmed by several degrees, large areas of the seafloor became starved of oxygen, and many marine invertebrates such as bivalves, brachiopods and ammonites suffered extinctions. Organic-rich black shales deposited at this time include Germany's Posidonia Shale at Holzmaden, famous for complete ichthyosaurs, some preserved with embryos and body outlines. The event lasted on the order of several hundred thousand years, though its precise duration is debated.

title: Earliest snakes
summary: Jaw fragments from Kirtlington, England, about 167 million years old, are among the oldest fossils attributed to snakes.
description: In 2015 Eophis underwoodi, from the Middle Jurassic Forest Marble Formation at Kirtlington in Oxfordshire, and several other Jurassic jaw fossils from England, Portugal and the United States were identified as early snakes, extending the group's fossil record back by some 70 million years. These animals are known only from fragments, so their body form is unknown, and some researchers question whether they are true snakes. Later fossils show that early snakes kept small hind limbs: Najash rionegrina from Argentina, about 95 million years old, had a sacrum and functional hind legs. Whether snakes first evolved on land, in burrows or in water has long been debated, with recent evidence favouring a terrestrial or burrowing origin.

title: Yanliao Biota: feathered dinosaurs before birds
summary: Volcanic lake beds in north-east China preserve feathered dinosaurs like Anchiornis, gliding mammals and insects from the Middle–Late Jurassic.
description: The Yanliao Biota, from the Jiulongshan and Tiaojishan formations of Liaoning, Hebei and Inner Mongolia, dates to roughly 165–157 million years ago and is preserved in fine-grained volcanic lake deposits. It includes Anchiornis, a crow-sized feathered paravian with long feathers on all four limbs, which in 2010 became the first dinosaur whose full plumage colours were reconstructed from fossil pigment structures. Its mammals reveal surprising diversity, including gliders such as Volaticotherium and Maiopatagium and the semi-aquatic Castorocauda. The tiny Juramaia, about 160 million years old, has been interpreted as an early relative of placental mammals, although its age and placement are disputed. Because these feathered dinosaurs predate Archaeopteryx, they answered the old objection that bird-like dinosaurs appear only after the first birds.

title: Morrison Formation: age of Jurassic giants
summary: Floodplains of the western US hosted Diplodocus, Brachiosaurus, Stegosaurus and Allosaurus, among the largest land animals that ever lived.
description: The Morrison Formation, a sequence of river, lake and floodplain sediments spread across about 1.5 million km² of the western United States, records a seasonally dry Late Jurassic landscape about 156–147 million years old. It is one of the world's richest sources of dinosaur fossils, including long-necked sauropods such as Diplodocus, Apatosaurus, Brontosaurus, Camarasaurus and Brachiosaurus, the plated Stegosaurus and the predators Allosaurus and Ceratosaurus. Sauropods here reached 25–30 m in length, and the coexistence of so many giant plant-eaters suggests they divided resources by feeding height and diet. Many species were first collected during the 'Bone Wars' rivalry between Othniel Marsh and Edward Drinker Cope in the late 19th century, and at Dinosaur National Monument, first excavated by Earl Douglass from 1909, about 1,500 bones remain exposed in the original quarry wall.

title: Tendaguru: Jurassic giants of East Africa
summary: Excavations at Tendaguru Hill in Tanzania uncovered Giraffatitan, one of the tallest dinosaurs, alongside the spiky stegosaur Kentrosaurus.
description: The Tendaguru Formation of south-eastern Tanzania preserves Late Jurassic coastal plain and tidal deposits closely comparable in age and fauna to North America's Morrison Formation. German expeditions between 1909 and 1913, relying on hundreds of local workers, shipped more than 200 tonnes of fossils to Berlin, and British expeditions followed in the 1920s. The finds include the sauropod Giraffatitan brancai, whose mounted skeleton in Berlin's Museum für Naturkunde stands about 13 m tall, as well as Dicraeosaurus, Tornieria, the stegosaur Kentrosaurus and the theropod Elaphrosaurus. The similarity to Morrison faunas shows that related dinosaur groups were still widespread across the former Pangaea in the Late Jurassic. The colonial-era collection is now part of discussions about restitution and recognition of Tanzanian labour.

title: Solnhofen lagoons preserve a Jurassic archipelago
summary: Fine-grained limestones of Bavaria preserve pterosaurs, Compsognathus, insects and jellyfish from Late Jurassic tropical lagoons.
description: The Solnhofen Limestone formed about 150 million years ago, early in the Tithonian stage of the Late Jurassic, in stagnant, hypersaline lagoons between reefs and islands on the northern margin of the Tethys Ocean, in what is now Bavaria, Germany. Low oxygen and high salinity on the lagoon floors excluded scavengers, so animals that washed or fell in were preserved in extraordinary detail, sometimes with soft tissues, wing membranes and even their final trackways. Besides Archaeopteryx, the deposits have yielded pterosaurs such as Rhamphorhynchus and Pterodactylus, the small dinosaur Compsognathus, fishes, horseshoe crabs, insects and jellyfish. The fine stone has been quarried for centuries and was used for lithographic printing after its invention in the 1790s.

title: Archaeopteryx, the 'first bird'
summary: Archaeopteryx combined feathered wings with teeth, clawed fingers and a long bony tail, a classic transitional fossil between dinosaurs and birds.
description: Archaeopteryx lived on the islands of the Solnhofen archipelago in Late Jurassic Bavaria about 150 million years ago and is known from more than a dozen skeletons and an isolated feather. Its first skeleton, the London specimen, was found and announced in 1861, just two years after Darwin's On the Origin of Species, and described in detail by Richard Owen in 1863; it quickly became a celebrated example of a transitional form between reptiles and birds. It had asymmetrical flight feathers like modern birds but also toothed jaws, three clawed fingers and a long bony tail, much like small theropod dinosaurs. Feathered dinosaurs found in China have since shown that many 'bird' features evolved earlier, and its exact position near the base of birds (Avialae) has been debated, though most analyses keep it among the earliest avialans. How well it could fly is also still discussed.

title: Archaeopteryx a forgery? Hoyle's claim (fringe)
dateLabel: c. 150 million years ago (age of the fossils; claim made in 1985)
summary: In 1985 astronomer Fred Hoyle and colleagues claimed the feathers on the London and Berlin Archaeopteryx fossils had been faked.
description: Beginning in 1985, a group including the astronomer Fred Hoyle, his collaborator Chandra Wickramasinghe and the physicist Lee Spetner published articles, first in the British Journal of Photography, arguing that the feather impressions on the London and Berlin specimens of Archaeopteryx had been forged. They suggested that a thin layer of artificial cement had been spread over genuine skeletons of a small dinosaur and that modern feathers were pressed into it, pointing to apparent differences in rock texture around the feathers and to features they said did not match between the slab and counterslab. Hoyle and Wickramasinghe expanded the argument in a 1986 book, and the claim was taken up for a time by some creationist writers. The London specimen, shown here at the Natural History Museum in London where it is kept, was the main focus of the dispute.
mainstreamView: Scientists at the Natural History Museum led by Alan Charig examined the London specimen and in 1986 showed in the journal Science that it is genuine: fine hairline cracks run continuously through the rock and the feather impressions and match exactly on both slabs, the cracks were old and filled with calcite, and mineral growths had formed over the surface before the fossil was found, none of which a later cement layer could explain. Most of the supposed evidence reflected unfamiliarity with how sediments turn to rock. Other Archaeopteryx skeletons with feather impressions have been found since, and feathered dinosaurs from China show that its mix of bird and dinosaur features is expected, so palaeontologists regard the forgery claim as refuted.

title: South Atlantic begins to open
summary: Paraná–Etendeka flood basalts erupted as South America began to separate from Africa, starting the birth of the South Atlantic Ocean.
description: Around 134–132 million years ago, the Paraná–Etendeka large igneous province erupted basalts that today cover more than a million square kilometres of southern Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay and Argentina, with a smaller counterpart on Namibia's Etendeka plateau. The eruptions are linked to the Tristan mantle hotspot and to rifting between South America and Africa. Seafloor spreading propagated northward from the south, and the two continents were fully separated along the equatorial Atlantic by roughly 105–100 million years ago. Matching coastlines, rock formations and fossils on either side of the South Atlantic later became key evidence for continental drift.

title: First flowering plants
summary: Angiosperms appear in the fossil record as pollen and small plants such as aquatic Montsechia, beginning a rise to dominate the world's floras.
description: The earliest widely accepted angiosperm fossils are pollen grains from the Valanginian–Hauterivian stages, roughly 135–130 million years ago, found in Israel, Italy and England. Early plant fossils include the aquatic Montsechia from Barremian rocks in Spain, roughly 130–125 million years old, and Archaefructus from China's Yixian Formation, about 125 million years old. Flowering plants remained minor parts of most floras until they diversified rapidly in the mid-Cretaceous, and by the end of the period they made up a large share of plant species, a shift sometimes called the Cretaceous Terrestrial Revolution. Molecular-clock studies often place angiosperm origins earlier, in the Jurassic or even the Triassic, and this mismatch with the fossil record, echoing Darwin's 'abominable mystery' about their sudden rise, is still unresolved.

title: Yixian Formation and the Jehol Biota
summary: Volcanic ash in Liaoning, China, buried feathered dinosaurs, early birds, mammals and flowers, transforming the story of how birds evolved.
description: The Yixian Formation of western Liaoning, dated to roughly 130–120 million years ago, preserves lake ecosystems repeatedly smothered by volcanic ash, producing fossils with feathers, fur, skin and stomach contents. In 1996 Sinosauropteryx became the first non-avian dinosaur described with feather-like filaments, and later finds included the 9-metre feathered tyrannosauroid Yutyrannus, thousands of the beaked bird Confuciusornis and, in the slightly younger Jiufotang Formation, the four-winged Microraptor. Mammals such as Repenomamus, one specimen of which was found with a young Psittacosaurus in its gut, and Eomaia show that some Mesozoic mammals were larger and more varied than once thought. The Jehol Biota also includes early flowering plants such as Archaefructus, along with insects, fishes and pterosaurs, making it one of the most important fossil windows on Earth.

title: Ontong Java Plateau erupts in the Pacific
summary: A vast submarine eruption in the western Pacific built a basalt plateau roughly the size of Alaska, the largest known large igneous province.
description: The Ontong Java Plateau, north of the Solomon Islands, is an oceanic plateau of basaltic crust up to about 30–35 km thick, formed mostly in a geologically brief episode around 122 million years ago, with possible later activity around 90 million years ago. Together with the Manihiki and Hikurangi plateaus, which may once have formed a single structure, it may represent the largest volcanic event preserved in the geological record. Its formation is commonly attributed to the head of a rising mantle plume, though alternatives, including unusual mantle melting or even an impact, have been proposed. The eruptions are widely linked to Oceanic Anoxic Event 1a, an episode of ocean warming, acidification and black shale deposition about 120 million years ago.

title: Humans walked with dinosaurs (fringe claim)
dateLabel: c. 113 million years ago (age of the Paluxy tracks)
summary: Some young-Earth creationists claim that human footprints lie beside dinosaur tracks along Texas's Paluxy River, proving the two lived together.
description: Since the 1930s, elongated impressions in the Early Cretaceous Glen Rose Formation along the Paluxy River near Glen Rose, Texas, have been promoted as giant human 'man tracks' alongside dinosaur footprints. The claim was popularised by creationist books and films in the 1970s and is often cited together with other alleged evidence, such as the Ica stones of Peru and the Acámbaro figures of Mexico, to argue that humans and non-avian dinosaurs lived together only a few thousand years ago. Proponents place this coexistence on a young-Earth timeline rather than in deep time; the entry is shown here at the age of the Glen Rose rocks.
mainstreamView: Detailed studies in the 1980s showed that the 'man tracks' are elongated dinosaur footprints with infilled toe marks, erosional features, or carvings made and sold locally during the Great Depression, and leading creationist organisations themselves stopped promoting them. Radiometric dating, the worldwide fossil succession and the complete absence of human or primate fossils in Mesozoic rocks show that non-avian dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago, more than 60 million years before the genus Homo appeared. The Ica stones and Acámbaro figures are modern artefacts. In a limited sense humans do share the planet with dinosaurs, because birds are living dinosaurs.

title: Kronosaurus and Australia's inland sea
summary: A shallow, cool inland sea covered much of eastern Australia, home to the giant short-necked pliosaur Kronosaurus and long-necked plesiosaurs.
description: In the Early Cretaceous, high sea levels flooded central and eastern Australia to form the Eromanga Sea, which lay at high southern latitudes and was at times cold enough for seasonal ice. Its deposits around Richmond and Hughenden in Queensland preserve the pliosaur Kronosaurus queenslandicus, one of the largest marine reptiles of its time at perhaps 9–10 m long, along with long-necked elasmosaurs, ichthyosaurs, turtles and the armoured dinosaur Kunbarrasaurus, whose carcass drifted out to sea. Plesiosaurs and ichthyosaurs had been top marine predators since the Triassic and Jurassic, a role taken over later in the Cretaceous by mosasaurs. The sea retreated by the early Late Cretaceous, leaving thick marine mudstones that now form the impermeable cap sealing water into the older sandstone aquifers of the Great Artesian Basin.

title: Polar dinosaurs of Victoria, Australia
summary: In Victoria, Australia, small dinosaurs like Leaellynasaura lived inside the Antarctic Circle, enduring weeks to months of continuous winter darkness.
description: In the Early Cretaceous, south-eastern Australia was still joined to Antarctica and lay at roughly 70–80° south. River deposits of the rift valley between the two continents, now exposed at Dinosaur Cove and other coastal sites in Victoria, have yielded small ornithopods such as the large-eyed, very long-tailed Leaellynasaura, along with theropods, early mammals and turtles. These animals endured long polar winters of twilight or darkness and cool climates, with evidence of seasonal freezing nearby. Excavations at Dinosaur Cove, led from 1984 by Thomas Rich and Patricia Vickers-Rich, required tunnelling into sea cliffs. The fauna is studied for clues to how dinosaurs coped with polar seasonality, including bone-growth patterns and possible warm-bloodedness.

title: Western Interior Seaway splits North America
summary: High Cretaceous sea levels flooded central North America, dividing it into Laramidia in the west and Appalachia in the east.
description: From roughly 100 million years ago, a shallow sea stretched from the Arctic Ocean to the Gulf of Mexico across the middle of North America, at its peak up to about 1,000 km wide and generally a few hundred metres deep. It split the continent into two landmasses, Laramidia in the west and Appalachia in the east, which developed partly distinct dinosaur faunas; the famous dinosaurs of Alberta, Montana and Utah lived on Laramidia's coastal plains. The seaway teemed with mosasaurs, plesiosaurs, sharks, the giant fish Xiphactinus and the flightless diving bird Hesperornis, while Pteranodon soared overhead, and the chalks of western Kansas, including Monument Rocks, preserve many of them. The sea gradually retreated in the latest Cretaceous as the Rocky Mountains rose during the Laramide orogeny and global sea levels fell.

title: Chalk seas: coccolithophores build the white cliffs
summary: Countless microscopic plates of coccolithophore algae piled up on flooded Late Cretaceous seafloors as chalk, which gave the Cretaceous its name.
description: Coccolithophores are single-celled marine algae that cover themselves with tiny calcium carbonate plates called coccoliths; their ancestors first appeared in the Late Triassic, and they became enormously abundant in the warm, high-sea-level oceans of the Late Cretaceous. On the flooded continental shelves their coccoliths, with the shells of foraminifera, settled as a fine white ooze that hardened into chalk, deposited across northern Europe, North America's Western Interior Seaway and elsewhere. The period takes its name from the Latin creta, 'chalk', after Jean-Baptiste d'Omalius d'Halloy named the chalky strata of the Paris Basin the 'terrain crétacé' in 1822. England's White Cliffs of Dover expose part of the Chalk Group, which reaches several hundred metres thick and records millions of years of slow accumulation. By burying vast amounts of carbon in seafloor carbonate, these plankton became a major part of the global carbon cycle; most coccolithophore species died out at the end-Cretaceous extinction, but some lineages survived and remain abundant today.

title: Pollinators and flowers: life in Burmese amber
summary: Myanmar amber about 99 million years old traps a pollen-dusted beetle, early direct evidence that insects were pollinating flowering plants.
description: Amber from the Hukawng Valley of northern Myanmar, dated by zircons to about 99 million years old, preserves mid-Cretaceous forest life in remarkable detail. A tiny tumbling flower beetle, Angimordella burmitina, described in 2019 with flowering-plant pollen on its body, is among the earliest direct evidence of insects pollinating angiosperms. Two amber insects once hailed as the oldest known bees, Melittosphex (2006) and Discoscapa (2020), have since been reclassified as wasps. As flowering plants diversified in the mid-Cretaceous, pollination by beetles, flies, wasps and later bees became increasingly important. The amber also preserves a feathered dinosaur tail, hatchling birds, lizards and frogs; since 2020 many palaeontologists and journals have avoided new Myanmar amber because its mining is linked to armed conflict and human-rights abuses in Kachin State.

title: Spinosaurus in North Africa's rivers
summary: The sail-backed, crocodile-snouted Spinosaurus, perhaps the longest predatory dinosaur, hunted fish in vast river systems of what is now the Sahara.
description: Spinosaurus aegyptiacus was first described by Ernst Stromer in 1915 from Egypt's Bahariya Oasis, but the original specimen was destroyed in an Allied bombing raid on Munich in 1944. Later finds, chiefly from the Kem Kem beds of south-eastern Morocco, show an animal perhaps 14 m long with a tall back sail, a long narrow snout, conical teeth suited to catching fish and an unusual paddle-like tail. The Kem Kem rivers, about 100–94 million years old, supported many large predators, including Carcharodontosaurus, alongside giant sawfish and coelacanths. How aquatic Spinosaurus was is actively debated: some researchers argue it pursued prey while swimming, while others see it as a wading, heron-like shoreline hunter.

title: Argentinosaurus and the titanosaur giants
summary: Titanosaurs in Patagonia such as Argentinosaurus may have weighed 70 tonnes or more, possibly the heaviest animals ever to walk on land.
description: Argentinosaurus huinculensis, from the Huincul Formation of Neuquén Province, Argentina, is known only from a few vertebrae, ribs and limb bones, but these are enormous: a single back vertebra is about 1.6 m tall. Mass estimates range from about 65 to more than 90 tonnes, making it a leading candidate for the largest land animal known, though such figures carry large uncertainties. Titanosaurs were the dominant sauropods of the Cretaceous, especially on the southern continents; relatives such as Patagotitan from Chubut, about 101 million years old, are known from more complete skeletons. Patagonian rocks of this age also yield giant predators such as Giganotosaurus and Mapusaurus.

title: Oceanic Anoxic Event 2 and the Cretaceous hothouse
summary: At the Cenomanian–Turonian boundary, oxygen-starved oceans buried vast organic carbon during one of the warmest intervals of the past 250 million years.
description: Around 94 million years ago, a pulse of volcanic carbon dioxide, probably from the Caribbean and other large igneous provinces, drove widespread ocean deoxygenation recorded by organic-rich black shales and a positive carbon-isotope excursion around the globe. The event, which lasted roughly half a million years, caused extinctions among plankton, ammonites and other marine life and is counted as a minor mass extinction. It occurred near the peak of the Cretaceous Thermal Maximum, when tropical sea surfaces may have exceeded 35 °C, the poles were largely or entirely ice-free and sea levels stood perhaps 100–250 m higher than today. The global reference section for the base of the Turonian stage is at Rock Canyon near Pueblo, Colorado, in sediments of the Western Interior Seaway.

title: Nemesis: a hidden star behind extinctions? (fringe)
dateLabel: c. 94 million years ago (one of the claimed periodic peaks)
summary: A 1984 hypothesis proposed that an unseen companion star of the Sun triggers comet showers and mass extinctions roughly every 26 million years.
description: In 1984 David Raup and Jack Sepkoski reported that marine extinction peaks over the past 250 million years, including Late Triassic, Jurassic, mid-Cretaceous (Cenomanian) and end-Cretaceous events, appeared to recur about every 26 million years. To explain this, two teams (Marc Davis, Piet Hut and Richard Muller; Daniel Whitmire and Albert Jackson) proposed that the Sun has a faint companion star, dubbed Nemesis, on a wide eccentric orbit that periodically disturbs the Oort cloud and sends showers of comets into the inner Solar System. Others suggested different periodic triggers, such as the Sun's oscillation through the galactic plane or a hypothetical distant planet. Proponents tied the end-Cretaceous impact to such a shower and predicted that the next one lies millions of years in the future.
mainstreamView: Nemesis was a serious, testable hypothesis published in Nature, but infrared all-sky surveys, notably NASA's WISE mission, and Gaia star data have found no companion star or brown dwarf of the kind it requires, and such a wide orbit would be destabilised by passing stars and galactic tides. Whether extinctions are periodic at all is disputed: many re-analyses with improved fossil databases and timescales find the signal weak or absent, and even researchers who still detect a roughly 27-million-year rhythm (such as Melott and Bambach in 2010) argue it is too regular to come from a star on a perturbed orbit. Most known impact craters do not line up with extinctions, and the end-Cretaceous extinction is linked to a single impact (Chicxulub) plus volcanism rather than to a demonstrated comet shower, so Nemesis is regarded as unsupported.

title: India breaks from Madagascar and heads north
summary: Rifting above the Marion hotspot split India from Madagascar, beginning India's rapid journey north across the Tethys Ocean toward Asia.
description: India, Madagascar and the Seychelles stayed joined for tens of millions of years after East Gondwana broke away from Africa, but around 90–84 million years ago a burst of volcanism, usually linked to the Marion mantle hotspot, accompanied their separation. Its traces include the flood basalts along Madagascar's eastern coast and in the south-west, and the columnar rhyolite of the St. Mary's Islands off south-western India. Once free, the Indian plate moved north at speeds that later reached about 15–20 cm per year, among the fastest plate motions known, as the Tethys Ocean closed ahead of it. Insular India carried its own Gondwanan plants and animals, with some exchange with other landmasses, until it reached Asia in the early Cenozoic, while Madagascar remained isolated, shaping its distinctive wildlife. Around 66–63 million years ago India passed over the Réunion hotspot, erupting the Deccan Traps and splitting from the Seychelles.

title: Zealandia splits from Gondwana
summary: Seafloor spreading opened the Tasman Sea, carrying Zealandia, a largely submerged continent that includes New Zealand, away from Australia and Antarctica.
description: In the mid-Cretaceous, extension along Gondwana's Pacific margin stretched and thinned a broad sliver of continental crust, and from about 84 million years ago seafloor spreading in the Tasman Sea began to carry it away from Australia and Antarctica. This block, Zealandia, covers almost 5 million km² but is about 94% under water, with New Zealand and New Caledonia as its main emergent parts; in 2017 geologists formally argued that it qualifies as Earth's eighth continent. Tasman Sea spreading continued until about 52 million years ago. Zealandia's long isolation shaped New Zealand's distinctive flora and fauna, though how much of its biota descends directly from Gondwanan ancestors is debated, because much of the region may have been submerged around 25–22 million years ago.

title: Laramide orogeny begins raising the Rockies
summary: Compression far inland from North America's Pacific margin began pushing up the ranges of the Rocky Mountains, such as Colorado's Front Range.
description: Beginning in the Late Cretaceous, roughly 80–70 million years ago, compression in western North America thrust up blocks of ancient basement rock to form ranges such as Colorado's Front Range, Wyoming's Wind River and Bighorn mountains and South Dakota's Black Hills, separated by deep, subsiding basins. Unusually, these uplifts lie 1,000 km or more from the plate boundary; the leading explanation is that the subducting Farallon plate flattened and slid at a shallow angle beneath the continent, possibly because a thick oceanic plateau was being subducted, though the mechanism is still debated. The rising land helped drive the retreat of the Western Interior Seaway, and the basins between the ranges filled with sediments that preserve the latest dinosaurs and early mammals. The orogeny continued into the Paleogene, ending around 55–35 million years ago, and although later uplift and erosion shaped today's peaks, the core ranges of the Rocky Mountains date from this episode.

title: The Fighting Dinosaurs of the Gobi
summary: A Velociraptor and a Protoceratops locked in combat were buried together, probably by a collapsing sand dune, in Mongolia's Gobi Desert.
description: The Djadochta Formation of Mongolia's Gobi Desert records a Late Cretaceous landscape of dune fields and seasonal streams. In 1971 a Polish–Mongolian expedition found the 'Fighting Dinosaurs' at Tugrikin Shireh: a Velociraptor with its sickle claw at the throat of a Protoceratops, which had clamped the predator's arm in its beak, the pair apparently buried alive. At nearby Bayanzag, the 'Flaming Cliffs', the American Museum expeditions led by Roy Chapman Andrews found the first fossils recognised as dinosaur eggs in 1923, along with the first Velociraptor. Eggs once credited to Protoceratops were later shown to belong to oviraptorids, so Oviraptor, named 'egg thief' in 1924, had probably been brooding its own nest.

title: Quetzalcoatlus, a giant of the skies
summary: In Texas, the azhdarchid pterosaur Quetzalcoatlus northropi reached a wingspan of about 10–11 m, among the largest flying animals ever.
description: Quetzalcoatlus was discovered in 1971 in the Javelina Formation of Big Bend National Park, Texas, in latest Cretaceous rocks about 68 million years old. It belonged to the azhdarchids, long-necked, toothless pterosaurs that probably stalked small prey on the ground like giant storks. With a wingspan estimated at 10–11 m and a body mass of perhaps 200–250 kg, it stood about as tall as a giraffe. How such giants became airborne has been debated; most researchers now think they launched with a powerful four-limbed leap. Pterosaurs, already reduced in diversity, disappeared entirely at the end-Cretaceous extinction.

title: Vegavis: modern birds before the asteroid
summary: Fossils from Antarctica's Vega Island show that relatives of today's waterfowl had already evolved before the end-Cretaceous extinction.
description: Vegavis iaai, first described in 2005 from Late Cretaceous rocks of Vega Island off the Antarctic Peninsula, is one of the few Mesozoic birds widely accepted as a member of the crown group that includes all living birds. A well-preserved Vegavis skull described in 2025 supported the genus's placement among early crown birds related to waterfowl and suggested it was a foot-propelled diver; in 2026 that skull was made the type specimen of a second species, Vegavis notopothousa. Together with Asteriornis, a roughly 66.7-million-year-old 'wonderchicken' from Belgium, Vegavis shows that the lineages of modern birds had begun to diversify before the end-Cretaceous extinction. Of the many bird groups alive at the time, only some crown birds survived, perhaps helped by small size and toothless beaks suited to eating seeds.

title: Mosasaurs rule the last Cretaceous seas
summary: Mosasaurs, giant marine lizards, ruled Late Cretaceous oceans; the first famous specimen came from chalk mines near Maastricht in the 18th century.
description: Mosasaurs appeared about 98 million years ago and within some 20 million years had become the top predators of Late Cretaceous seas, after ichthyosaurs had died out, sharing the oceans with plesiosaurs and large sharks. A huge skull found in chalk mines at Sint-Pietersberg near Maastricht around 1780 was seized by French troops in 1794 and helped Georges Cuvier argue that species could become extinct. Named Mosasaurus hoffmannii after the river Meuse (Latin Mosa), the animal reached perhaps 12 m or more, and the Maastrichtian, the last stage of the Cretaceous, is named after the rocks of this region. Mosasaurs died out completely in the end-Cretaceous extinction.

title: Tyrannosaurus rex and the Hell Creek world
summary: Tyrannosaurus rex, a 12-metre, bone-crushing predator, hunted Triceratops and Edmontosaurus on the floodplains of western North America.
description: Tyrannosaurus lived in western North America during roughly the last two to three million years of the Cretaceous; the first skeleton recognised as such was found by Barnum Brown in the Hell Creek Formation of Montana in 1902 and named by Henry Fairfield Osborn in 1905. Adults reached about 12 m long and perhaps 8–9 tonnes, had one of the strongest bites of any land animal and could crush bone, and growth rings show they grew extremely fast in their teens. The Hell Creek fauna also included Triceratops, Edmontosaurus, Ankylosaurus and Pachycephalosaurus, as well as early mammals and birds, and its sediments record the Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary itself. Whether some smaller specimens are juvenile T. rex or a separate, smaller tyrannosaur, Nanotyrannus, was long debated; studies published in 2025, including one of a near-complete skeleton from the 'Dueling Dinosaurs' fossil, concluded that Nanotyrannus is a distinct genus, although some researchers still dispute this.

title: Deccan Traps erupt in India
summary: Enormous flood-basalt eruptions in west-central India spanned the end-Cretaceous extinction, building lava piles more than 2 km thick.
description: The Deccan Traps, one of the largest volcanic provinces on Earth, today cover about 500,000 km² of west-central India, with stacked lava flows more than 2 km thick in the Western Ghats; their original extent was much larger. Most of the volume erupted within roughly a million years around the Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary, as the Indian plate passed over the Réunion hotspot. High-precision dating shows that major eruptions began a few hundred thousand years before the Chicxulub impact and continued afterwards. How much the volcanic carbon dioxide and sulphur contributed to the end-Cretaceous extinction, compared with the impact, is actively debated: most researchers see the asteroid as the main trigger, while volcanism may have stressed ecosystems beforehand and slowed recovery.

title: Chicxulub asteroid impact
summary: An asteroid about 10 km wide struck the Yucatán Peninsula, gouging a 180-km crater and causing global darkness, cooling and possibly widespread fires.
description: The Chicxulub crater, about 180 km across and buried beneath Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula and the Gulf of Mexico, was formed by the impact of an asteroid roughly 10 km wide. The impact released energy equivalent to billions of Hiroshima bombs, generating megatsunamis, earthquakes and ejecta that rained down worldwide, possibly igniting widespread fires. Vaporised sulphur-rich rock, dust and soot filled the stratosphere, blocking sunlight for years, collapsing photosynthesis and causing a severe 'impact winter'. In 1980 Luis and Walter Alvarez and colleagues attributed a global iridium-rich boundary layer to an impact; the buried structure had been noticed in Pemex oil-exploration data by Glen Penfield in 1978 and reported with Antonio Camargo in 1981, and in 1990–1991 Alan Hildebrand and colleagues identified it as the impact site, whose age matches the extinction to within a few tens of thousands of years. Drilling in 2016 sampled its peak ring, and fossils at the Tanis site in North Dakota may record the first hours after the impact.

title: End-Cretaceous (K–Pg) mass extinction
summary: About three-quarters of species died out, including all non-avian dinosaurs, pterosaurs and ammonites, ending the Mesozoic Era.
description: The Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction removed an estimated 75% of plant and animal species. Non-avian dinosaurs, pterosaurs, mosasaurs, plesiosaurs and ammonites vanished entirely, while marine plankton, flowering plants, mammals, birds, lizards and snakes also suffered heavy losses. The boundary is marked worldwide by a thin clay layer enriched in iridium, shocked quartz and impact spherules, first highlighted in 1980 using rocks from Gubbio, Italy, and elsewhere. The consensus view is that the Chicxulub impact was the principal cause, with Deccan volcanism a possible contributing stressor whose role is still debated. Survivors, especially mammals and birds, radiated rapidly in the Paleogene, opening the Cenozoic 'Age of Mammals'.

title: Shiva crater: a second K–Pg impact? (fringe)
summary: Palaeontologist Sankar Chatterjee proposed that a huge seafloor basin off Mumbai is an impact crater formed at the same time as Chicxulub.
description: Beginning in the 1990s, Sankar Chatterjee and colleagues argued that the Bombay High area on India's western continental shelf and the surrounding basin conceal an impact structure roughly 600 km long and 400 km wide, named Shiva after the Hindu god of destruction and renewal. They proposed that it formed about 66 million years ago, around the time of the Chicxulub impact, and that it may have intensified Deccan volcanism and helped split the Seychelles from India. The area is a major offshore oil-producing region, so its buried geology has been mapped in detail by petroleum exploration.
mainstreamView: The structure has not been accepted as an impact crater: no shocked minerals, impact melt or other diagnostic impact evidence has been found, and its shape and gravity signature are explained by rifting, faulting and volcanism as India passed over the Réunion hotspot and separated from the Seychelles. It is not listed in the Earth Impact Database, and Chicxulub alone accounts for the global K–Pg impact layer.
